doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Musicians' union reaction to the mellotron and synthesizers
summary: The union was slow to understand recording, banned the awkward mellotron, and was slow on synthesizers while musicians were angrier.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Was there any noise — no pun intended — from the musicians’ union about the rise of synthesizers in the studio?

Yeah there was a lot. The union, their focus has always been within — their boundaries are defined by things that they understand which traditionally has been Broadway shows, weddings, club dates. And they never really related well to the recording scene. They’re actually better at it now. But by the time they caught up it was too late. I remember in the 70s there was an instrument called the mellotron, which was a keyboard instrument and it was a bear. It was like it was a real beast. And it had, each key was connected to a strip of recording tape, so you pressed the key and that tape, the recording tape would be pushed down on a capstan, or rotor, and the tape would play. And the noise would only last, I think it was seven or eight seconds or something. It was an actual recording of a violin or a flute. In reality the recordings first of all weren’t very good. And also the tapes would start stretching almost immediately. So this thing didn’t sound anything like string section. It had its own sound, which the Beatles used it a lot, but they used it in — and why is of course back to George Martin’s skill as a producer — but they always used it in ways that they weren’t trying to sound like a string section.
It was just its own thing.

They did the effect of strings doing some things. So it came and there was a big splash — it was very expensive instrument. And clearly it was not going to replace any string players because it was just a beast. It was always out of tune. It was the action — there was no action at all, it was impossible to play. To play a run — forget it. It was useless. But the union, after a while it took them like six months to a year, but suddenly they came out with this edict, mellotrons are illegal on session, because it’s going to put string players out of work. They completely missed the point that everybody tried it said this thing’s terrible. We’re not going to use it. Nobody wanted to use it except as an effect. That’s kind of where they’ve been at. Synthesizers, it took them a long time to understand them. They are really capable of a lot of unique sounds that couldn’t be done by other instruments. But there is a certain amount of imitating of other instruments which was a sore spot with musicians. I think musicians were more angry than the union, which it took them years before they took any kind of a stance and then it didn’t really matter.
